papers.title: Microbial arsenic transformations and their biogeochemical implications.
papers.journal: Microbiology and molecular biology reviews : MMBR
papers.abstract: SUMMARYThe ubiquity and toxicity of arsenic (As) have exerted strong selective pressure on microbial life, driving the evolution of specialized resistance pathways. The speciation of As strongly affects its mobility and toxicity. Virtually all extant microorganisms possess genes that act specifically on inorganic As-arsenite (AsIII) and arsenate (AsV)-to improve fitness in its presence. The use of As in microbial metabolism via AsV reduction or AsIII oxidation has been well documented, but remains relatively rare. However, virtually all microorganisms can detoxify inorganic As via the reduction of AsV and the efflux of AsIII, a well-characterized pathway encoded in the ars operon. Some can also methylate As, converting AsIII into monomethylarsenite (MMAsIII), dimethylarsenite (DMAsIII), and trimethylarsine (TMAsIII). Since TMAsIII is volatile, the transformation has potential for bioremediation applications. However, the biotic and abiotic factors conducive to As methylation in the environment are poorly understood. The gene encoding the responsible enzyme (arsM) is relatively widespread among both aerobic and anaerobic species, but the latter show limited methylation efficiencies in pure culture. Despite the ancient origins of the arsM gene-dating back to before the Great Oxidation Event-the biological role of As methylation in microorganisms remains unclear. In flooded soils, As methylation is enhanced, which results in higher environmental toxicity-MMAsIII and DMAsIII being more toxic than AsIII. Therefore, resistance pathways, such as efflux, demethylation, and oxidation, have evolved to specifically cope with such products. In contrast, some microorganisms can reduce MMAsV and DMAsV. It is assumed that the ability to produce and release MMAsIII and DMAsIII confers a competitive advantage because these may inhibit surrounding species. papers.title: Naegele's rule is not a 280-day count: generative AI conflates two distinct pregnancy-dating algorithms.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Naegele's calendar rule and an exact 280-day count are commonly treated as equivalent methods for estimating the due date (EDD), although their calendar arithmetic differs. We quantified this difference and evaluated whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems disclosed and accurately labeled the method used. METHODS: A deterministic script calculated EDDs for every last menstrual period (LMP) date from January 1, 1812, through December 31, 2025, using Naegele's calendar rule and a fixed 280-day count. Five generative AI systems answered four prespecified LMP prompts, representing agreement and differences of 1, 2, and 3 days. Each prompt was submitted in three separate conversations, yielding 60 responses. RESULTS: Among 78,163 LMP dates, the methods produced identical EDDs in 34,609 cases (44.3 %) and different EDDs in 43,554 (55.7 %). Naegele's calendar rule produced dates 1 day later in 27.0 %, 2 days later in 21.0 %, and 3 days later in 7.7 %. The methods never agreed among 14,828 intervals containing February 29. Of 60 AI responses, 57 (95.0 %) included the exact 280-day date and 48 (80.0 %) stated a calculation method. Only 18 of 45 responses to divergent dates distinguished the algorithms. Twelve of 48 method-stating responses contained a method-label mismatch. CONCLUSIONS: Naegele's calendar rule and fixed 280-day counting are distinct algorithms. Their small numerical differences are unlikely to be clinically important, but they provide a deterministic test of computational transparency. Generative AI systems should disclose the calculation used, distinguish non-equivalent methods, and label them accurately.

papers.title: Allopatric speciation of Oroperipatus velvet worms driven by Andean orogenesis and paleoclimate.
papers.abstract: The role of Andean orogeny in the diversification of ancient, low-vagility terrestrial invertebrates remains poorly understood. Herein, we examined Andean onychophorans (Oroperipatus) to evaluate how climatic change and vicariant processes associated with Andean uplift influenced speciation and their disjunct distribution across the Americas. Morphological and molecular analyses of 13 species sampled across the taxon's range revealed strong concordance between geography and phylogenetic structure, identifying two main lineages gathering eastern (Amazonian) and western (Pacific) Andean species, respectively. Divergence-time analyses suggest that these two lineages predate major Andean uplift and were likely shaped by paleoclimatic and vegetational changes. Later diversification was probably driven by climatic, ecological, and vicariant processes linked to the diachronous rise of the Andes. Close relationship among Ecuadorian, Galápagos, and Mexican species suggests stepwise dispersal via transient Pacific islands or independent Miocene-Pliocene overwater dispersal from Ecuador. Ten new species are described, increasing known Oroperipatus diversity by ∼50%.

papers.title: Thermochemistry and Tunneling Enhance the PCET Reactivity of Ni and Cu Complexes With Redox-Active Ligands.
papers.abstract: Herein, we report the synthesis, characterization, and reactivity of Cu-acetate and Ni-acetate complexes bound by tridentate redox-active ligands capable of reaching three molecular oxidation states. The reduced complexes ([XMOAc]2-) were characterized by single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis, depicting metal-acetate cores stabilized by intramolecular H-bonding interactions. Cyclic voltammetry measurements indicate that [XMOAc]2- can be reversibly oxidized to [XMOAc]- and [XMOAc], and that the reduction potentials varied depending on the ligand substitution. The oxidation of [XMOAc]2- to [XMOAc]- and [XMOAc] was accomplished using 1 and 2 equiv of ferrocenium, respectively. The proton-coupled electron transfer reactivity of the oxidized complexes was analyzed in detail. Thermochemical analysis determined that the [XMOAc] species had higher affinities toward H atom equivalents than [XMOAc]-, and that the systems with electron-withdrawing groups were more prone to undergo reductive protonation. The kinetics for the reactions of [XMOAc]- and [XMOAc] with TEMPOH (1-hydroxy-2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine) showed that the [XNiOAc]- complexes depict enhanced reaction rates. These findings contradict our thermochemical analysis (i.e., complexes with higher thermodynamic tendency to accept H atoms usually react faster) and are explained by tunneling effects. Further analysis of the PCET reactions provided further evidence that nonthermodynamic factors govern the PCET reactivity of the Ni-semiquinone oxidants.

papers.title: Electrochemically Passivated Liquid Metal Printing for Two-Dimensional Wafer-Scale, Atomically-Thin Non-Layered Oxides.
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) non-layered metal oxides (NMOs) are promising for advanced electronics and catalysis owing to their tunable electronic structures and highly active surfaces. However, synthesizing wafer-scale, atomically thin NMOs is challenging due to their intrinsic isotropic bonding. Here, we present an electrochemical passivation liquid metal printing strategy that regulates oxidation kinetics via galvanic coupling, enabling the synthesis of wafer-scale, atomically thin NMOs in air. Critically, using aluminum foil as both a sacrificial anode and a high-surface-energy substrate enables a self-limiting oxidation reaction and produces wafer-scale and uniform α-Bi2O3 films with thickness down to 0.7 nm when coupled with ultralow contact-angle wetting (13.8°). This method demonstrates broad applicability, facilitating the synthesis of ultrathin films of various NMOs, including Ga2O3 (1 nm), In2O3 (1.5 nm), and ZnO (1.7 nm). Notably, the quantum confinement and abundant active sites in the 2D α-Bi2O3 film enhance its light-harvesting and promote charge separation, resulting in a photocatalytic degradation efficiency of 98.6% with a rate constant of 0.0355 min-1. This work provides a scalable strategy for synthesizing large-area, ultrathin 2D NMOs, establishing a foundation for their applications in next-generation photocatalysis.

papers.title: Deterministic Noncontact Release and Transfer Through Programmable Interfacial Stress Reconfiguration.
papers.abstract: Deterministic placement of fragile microcomponents is a central challenge in advanced electronic manufacturing, including chiplet integration and micro-LED assembly. Most switchable adhesives rely on contact-mediated detachment, which concentrates stress at the perimeter and causes slip and misalignment. Here, we report a diving beetle-inspired electroactive switchable adhesive (DESA) that achieves deterministic transfer through vibration-driven noncontact release enabled by interfacial stress reconfiguration. A perforated electrode couples a bioinspired adhesive layer to an electroactive PVC gel actuator, defining electrically contracting electrode-contact regions and mechanically linked gel-continuous hole regions. Under actuation, differential displacement between these regions deforms the adhesive layer and promotes partial peel-off at distributed interior sites rather than along a single perimeter front. At the 269 Hz resonance, vibration amplifies the displacement mismatch and spreads peel-off across the contact area, progressively reducing the load-bearing area. The resulting inertial stress completes noncontact separation, suppressing misalignment. The adhesive layer provides > 20 kPa dry and > 42 kPa wet adhesion across diverse substrates and retains stable performance over 1000 attachment-detachment cycles. On a robotic platform, the device transfers microcomponents with a lateral placement error of 318 ± 155 µm (≈99.5% placement accuracy). This interfacial stress reconfiguration offers a route to deterministic placement beyond adhesion-strength control.

papers.title: A Global Overview of Interventions to Enhance Resilience Among Families with Pregnant Women: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pregnancy affects the entire family system, yet resilience-oriented perinatal interventions may target either maternal capacities or family processes. The extent to which existing interventions address individual or family-system resilience has not been comprehensively mapped. OBJECTIVE: To map the characteristics, components, outcomes, and orientation of resilience-enhancing interventions involving pregnant women and/or their families worldwide. METHODS: This scoping review followed the Arksey and O'Malley framework. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and EBSCOhost were searched from inception to April 2026. No geographical restrictions were applied. Empirical studies evaluating resilience-enhancing interventions involving pregnant women or families during the perinatal period were eligible. RESULTS: Of 3687 records identified, 1439 underwent title and abstract screening; 1403 were excluded at this stage, and 20 of 30 full-text reports were excluded. Ten studies came from database searching and one from hand searching. Eleven studies from Iran, Pakistan, the United States, and Belgium were included. Six intervention types were identified: structured resilience training, antenatal education, kangaroo mother care, coparenting programs, family therapy, and community-based psychosocial support. Common components included psychoeducation, emotional regulation, coping skills, relationship strengthening, optimism, communication, and collaborative problem-solving. Most interventions targeted maternal resilience at the individual level. Only family therapy and coparenting programs explicitly positioned the family as the unit of care. Reported outcomes were mixed, with positive findings in some studies, null between-group effects in others, and variable strength of evidence. CONCLUSIONS: The globally eligible evidence base remains fragmented, geographically concentrated, and predominantly focused on individual resilience. papers.title: "Twisted Reality": Covert Psychological Abuse in Intimate Partner Violence, A Framework for Understanding Tactics and Retaliatory Escalation.
papers.abstract: Covert psychological abuse (CPA) in intimate partner relationships, encompassing tactics such as gaslighting, ghosting, and projection, constitutes a pervasive and underrecognized form of harm. Despite growing clinical awareness, little is known about what occurs when survivors confront their abusive partners about this behavior within an ongoing relationship. The present study aimed to document the forms of CPA experienced by survivors and to examine the responses that followed. In-depth individual interviews and focus group sessions were conducted with 67 Jewish Canadian women survivors of CPA and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Of the 67 participants, 59 (88%) reported having directly confronted their partners about the abusive behavior, while 8 (12%) had not done so. Two primary themes were identified: (a) a foundational repertoire of covert control tactics that eroded survivors' trust in their own perceptions (gaslighting, stonewalling and ghosting, and projection) and (b) a pattern of punitive escalation, encompassing prolonged silent treatment, smear campaigns, and hoovering, triggered specifically by survivors' acts of confrontation. Most participants who confronted their partners reported an intensification rather than a reduction of CPA in its aftermath. Findings are discussed within two-tiered theoretical frameworks: Coercive control theory and narcissistic trait patterns in the partner abuse literature, underscoring the need for clinical frameworks that recognize confrontation as a potential escalation point.
